parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian -esco. Doublet of -ais and -ois.

parole.significato: suffix used to build absolute superlative forms of adjectives
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian -ìssimo, from Latin -issimus. First attested in the 16th century.
Borrowed from Italian agrume, borrowed from Latin ācrūmen.
Borrowed from Italian amabile. Doublet of aimable.
Borrowed from Italian amaretto, from amaro (“bitter”) (from Latin amārus) + diminutive ending -etto.
Borrowed from Italian arcata. By surface analysis, arc + -ade.
Borrowed from Italian aria.
Borrowed from Italian artigiano, Inherited from Vulgar Latin *artītiānus, from Latin artītus (“skilled”), past participle of artiō (“to instruct in arts”), from ars (“art, skill”).
Borrowed from Italian attitudine (“attitude, aptness”), from Medieval Latin aptitūdō (“aptitude”) (whence French aptitude) and actitūdō (“acting, posture”).

parole.significato: stick, rod, any long thin object
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian bacchetta.
Borrowed from Italian balcone.
Inherited from Middle French, from Italian balaustro, from Latin balaustĭum. See English baluster for more.
Inherited from Middle French barque, probably borrowed from Italian barca or a Medieval Latin equivalent, from Late Latin barca. Doublet of barge.
Borrowed from Italian bene.
Borrowed from Italian brillare.
Borrowed from Italian broccoli, plural of broccolo, diminutive of brocco (“shoot, sprout”), from Latin broccus, of Gaulish origin.
Inherited from Old French bufle, from Italian bufalo, from Vulgar Latin *būfalus, variant form of Latin būbalus, from Ancient Greek βούβαλος (boúbalos).
Borrowed from Italian busto, from Latin būstum.
A Frenchification (see carré) of Italian bequadro, itself derived from Medieval Latin b quadrātum (“B natural”, literally “square B”).

Borrowed from Italian cabriola, cabriole (“horse caper”) + -et, from Latin capreolus, from Proto-Indo-European *kápros (“buck, he-goat”); see also Old Norse hafr (“he-goat”), Old English hæfer, Welsh gafr, Old Irish gabor. Doublet of Chevrolet.
Borrowed from Italian quadro (“framed painting, square”), from Latin quadrum, from quattuor (“four”). Cf. Old French querre, inherited from the same source; see also carre.

parole.significato: tracing (the reproduction of an image made by copying it through translucent paper)
parole.testo: Deverbal from calquer, borrowed from Italian calcare, from Latin calcāre (“to tread”).

parole.significato: to model, to imitate, to copy
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian calcare, from Latin calcāre.
Probably borrowed from Italian campagna, itself from Late Latin campania, from Latin campus.
From Italian cammeo, from Medieval Latin camaeus.
Inherited from Middle French canaille, from Italian canaglia.
Borrowed from Italian cantatrice, from Latin cantātrīcem.
Borrowed from Italian cappuccino, ultimately from Late Latin cappa (“cape, hood”).
Borrowed from Italian cartello, diminutive of carta, from Latin carta. Related to English card.
Borrowed from Italian carena (cf. Ligurian carena), from Latin carīna.
Borrowed from Italian cassa, from Latin capsa. Doublet of châsse and caisse.
From Italian castrato, from Latin castrō (“to castrate”), likely from caedō (“to cut”).
Borrowed from Italian catafalco, from Vulgar Latin *catafalicum, from Ancient Greek κατά (katá, “down”) + Latin fala (“scaffolding, wooden siege tower”), which is from Etruscan. Doublet of échafaud.
Borrowed from Italian chianti, after Chianti, its area of production. Through Latin from the Etruscan 𐌂𐌋𐌀𐌍𐌕𐌄 (clante).

parole.significato: team or group of galley slaves
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian ciurma, from Late Latin celeusma, from Ancient Greek κέλευσμα (kéleusma).

parole.significato: Poor Clare, a nun of the Order of Saint Clare
parole.testo: From Italian and Latin clarissa (“Poor Clare”), from Clara + -issa (“-ess”).
Borrowed from Italian collina, from Late Latin collina, from Latin collinus.

From colmate (“land for filling”), from Italian colmata (“filled”), from Latin cumulāre, form of cumulō (“to heap, fill”); compare cumulus (“a heap”). Cognate to Italian colmare; Spanish and Portuguese colmar.
Borrowed from Italian confidente

From earlier coqueluchon (“a kind of monk's cowl or hood”), from Italian coccolucio, from Latin cucullus (“hood”). Sufferers of the 1510 influenza pandemic would wear a hood resembling the coqueluchon. The spelling and/or "whooping cough" sense may have been influenced by coq (“rooster”), from the c
Borrowed from Italian corsaro, from Medieval Latin cursārius (“pirate”). Doublet of coursier.

parole.significato: a style of dress characteristic of a particular country, period or people
parole.testo: PIE word  *ḱóm  PIE word  *swé Borrowed from Italian costume, from Latin cōnsuētūdinem (“custom, habit”). Doublet of consuétude and coutume.
Borrowed from Italian credito, from Latin crēditum.
Inherited from Middle French desseigner, borrowed from Italian disegnare, from Latin designāre. Doublet of désigner.
From Italian diana, from Latin Diana.
Borrowed from Italian ditto, a variant of detto (past participle of dire (“to say”)), from Latin dicere.
From Italian, from Latin, the feminine form of dīvus (“divine one; deified mortal”).
From Italian dogale, from Late Latin ducalis (“ducal”). Doublet of ducal.

parole.significato: title of respect given to certain monks and other religious figures
parole.testo: Borrowing from Italian don or older dom, from Latin dominus (“master”). Cognate with English don.
Inherited from Middle French, from late Old French, borrowed from Italian ducato, from Medieval Latin ducātus, from dux (“duke; leader”). Doublet of duché and dogat.

parole.significato: cathedral of a town or city, especially in Italy or Germany
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French domme, dome, borrowed from Italian duomo, from Latin domus (ecclesiae) (literally “house (of the church)”), a calque of Ancient Greek οἶκος τῆς ἐκκλησίας (oîkos tês ekklēsías).
Borrowed from Italian incastrare, from Late Latin incastrāre, from Latin castrum (“fortress”). Unrelated to French castrer (“to castrate”).
Borrowed from Italian scala, from Latin scāla. Doublet of échelle, which was inherited.
Borrowed from Italian spianata with influx from Spanish explanada, both from Latin explānātus.
From Italian stufata (“stew”), from Latin extufare, from Ancient Greek τύφος (túphos, “steam”). Compare Italian stufato, Greek στιφάδο (stifádo).

parole.significato: A type of small light green kidney-shaped bean, common in France.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian fagiolo (“bean”), from Latin phaseolus (“bean”), diminutive form of phasēlus, from Ancient Greek φάσηλος (phásēlos, “bean”).
Borrowed from Italian flemma, from Latin phlegma (“phlegm”), one of the four bodily humours, thought to cause a sluggish and unemotional nature. First attested in the late 1700s. Doublet of flegme.
Borrowed from Italian fonda (“purse”), from Latin funda (“leather pocket, sling”).
From Middle French (16th century), from Italian foga, from Latin fuga. Doublet of fugue.

Via Middle French frise, derived in a textile sense from friser (“to curl”) or related to the demonym Frisian due to import via Northern ships, and in an architecture sense from an Upper Italian fris f, Medieval Latin frisum, frisium, frigium, frixum, of controversial origin, possibly from multiple
Borrowed from Italian frusto (“morsel”), from Latin frustum.

Ca. 1600, borrowed in the musical sense from Italian fuga, itself a borrowing from Latin fuga. Doublet of fougue (from the inherited Italian cognate). The sense “flight” (18th c.) may be a new borrowing from the Italian.
Borrowed from Italian golfo, from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin colfus, culfus, alteration of colpus, from Ancient Greek κόλπος (kólpos). Doublet of gouffre.

parole.significato: cave (a large, naturally occurring cavity formed underground)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian grotta, from Latin crypta. Doublet of crypte.
From Italian gruppo, itself derived from Vulgar Latin *cruppus.

From Middle French grège (“(adjective) of silk: raw, unfinished; of the colour of such silk, greyish-beige; (noun) raw or unfinished silk; the colour of such silk, greyish-beige”), from Italian greggio (“raw, unrefined; unbleached”); further etymology uncertain, possibly from Vulgar Latin *gregius (
From Italian incarnato, from Latin incarnātus. Doublet of incarné. By surface analysis, incarner + -at.

From infanterie (“infantry”) + -iste, from Italian infanteria, from infante, fante (“a knave, footman, foot soldier”), from Latin īnfāns (“infant”); an exact cognate of Dutch infanterist and German Infanterist.
Inherited from Middle French jovial, borrowed from Italian gioviale, from Late Latin Ioviālis. Unrelated to joie.
Borrowed from Italian lasagna.
Borrowed from Italian lento. Doublet of lent.
Inherited from Middle French ligue, from Italian lega, from the verb legare, from Latin ligō (“to tie”).

Probably a borrowing from Italian liscio (“smooth, polished”). Other theories include a crossing of Latin lixāre (presumably related to lixa (“lye”)) and allīsus (“crushed against”). See also Spanish and Portuguese liso, Catalan llis, Italian liscio.
Borrowed from Italian lista
Borrowed from Italian maestro, from Latin magistrum. Doublet of magister, borrowed from Latin, maître, inherited from Latin, and master, borrowed from English.
Borrowed from Italian maggiordomo, from Late Latin maior domūs (“steward”), from Latin maior (“main, principal”) + genitive singular of domus (“household”).
From Italian manganese, alteration of Medieval Latin magnēsia.

parole.significato: only used in à la manque
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian manco, from Latin mancus.
From Italian macchietta (“speck, little spot”), diminutive of macchia (“spot”), ultimately from Latin macula (“spot, stain”).

From Italian merlone (“merlon”), from merlo (“merlon”) + -one (suffix forming augmentatives). Merlo is derived from Late Latin merulus, merlus, possibly from Latin merula (“blackbird”) (as merlons resemble a row of birds perched on a wall), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ems- (“black; blackbird”).

PIE word  *médʰyos Borrowed from Italian mezzanino, from mezzano (“(adjective) middle; (noun) go-between”) + -ino (diminutive suffix). Mezzano is derived from Latin mediānus (“central, middle”, adjective), from medius (“mid, middle”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *médʰyos (“middle”)) + -ānus
Directly from Italian minestrone, from minestra (“soup”, ultimately from Latin ministrō) + -one (augmentative suffix).
Borrowed from Italian mira, from Latin mīrō (“to wonder at”).
Borrowed from Italian medaglia. Doublet of maille.

parole.significato: Neapolitan (of, from or relating to the city of Naples, capital and largest city of Campania, Italy, or the surrounding…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian napoletano, from Latin neāpolītānus, from Neāpolis, from Ancient Greek Νεάπολις (Neápolis, literally “new city”) (whence Naples).

Often considered a borrowing from Italian niello (from Latin nigellus), but may also reflect a deverbal of nieller, inherited from the same Latin source, perhaps nevertheless influenced in its spelling by Italian.
Borrowed from Italian nocchiero, from Latin nauclērus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek ναύκληρος (naúklēros).
Borrowed from Italian nunzio (with phonetic adaptations), itself borrowed from Latin nuntius (“messenger”).
Borrowed from Italian ombrello, ombrella, from Late Latin umbrella, or formed from ombre + -elle, based on Latin umbella (whence French ombelle was borrowed), from umbra (“shade”). See ombre.
Borrowed from Italian opera, from Latin opera. Doublet of œuvre and opus.
Borrowed from Italian oratorio. Doublet of oratoire.
Borrowed from Italian ortolano, from Latin hortulānus (“gardener”). Doublet of hortelain, found in regional usage.
From Italian pagliaccio, from paglia (“straw”), from Latin palea.
Borrowed from Italian paladino, from Latin palatīnus. Doublet of palatin.
From Italian palanco, variant of paranco (“hoist”), from Vulgar Latin palanca, alteration of Latin phalanga. See also palanque, planche, palanche.

parole.significato: Palermitan (native or inhabitant of the city of Palermo, Sicily, Italy) (usually male)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian palermitano, from Latin Panormitānus, from Panormus + -itānus.

parole.significato: Palermitan (of, from or relating to the city of Palermo, Sicily, Italy)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian palermitano, from Latin Panormitānus, from Panormus + -itānus.
Inherited from Middle French pennache (“plume of feathers”), borrowed from Italian pennacchio, from Late Latin pinnāculum. Doublet of pinacle.
Via Italian para-, from parare, from Latin parō (“to shield”).

From Italian pastello (“pastel”), from Medieval Latin pastellum (“dough, paste”), from Latin pasta (“dough, paste”), ultimately from Ancient Greek παστός (pastós, “dough, paste”). Doublet of pastille.

Borrowed from Italian pasticcio (“pie, something blended”), from Vulgar Latin *pastīcius, from Late Latin pasta, from Ancient Greek παστά (pastá, “barley porridge”), from παστός (pastós, “sprinkled with salt”). Doublet of pastis, which was borrowed through Occitan.

parole.significato: patina, an oxidation like on bronze or similar effect
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian patina, itself from Latin patina (“plate, pan”).
From Italian pergola.
16th century in the sense of "pestle", borrowed from Italian pistone (15th century), from Latin pistō (“to pound”), from the root of pīnsō (“to crush”).
Borrowed from Italian polenta.

parole.significato: ointment (a thick viscous preparation for application to the skin, often containing medication)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian pomata, from pomo (“apple”), as such ointments were originally made from apples, from Latin pōmum.
Borrowed from Italian porcospino, from Vulgar Latin *porcospinus, calque of Ancient Greek ἀκανθόχοιρος (akanthókhoiros), from ἄκανθα (ákantha, “spine”) + χοῖρος (khoîros, “pig”).

parole.significato: cowrie, a mollusk of the family Cypraeidae, or its translucent shell
parole.testo: From Old French (1298 AD) pourcelaine (“cowrie, cockle, or similar univalve seashell; the polished material of these shells”). By metaphorical extension, also fine china, which had a similar appearance. From Italian (13th century, in Marco Polo) porcellana (“cowrie; china; vagina”). From porcella (“
Borrowed from Italian posticcio, from Late Latin appositīcius, from Latin appōnō (“put or place near”).

parole.significato: a small farm animal (not necessarily a sheep)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian pecora, from Latin pecus.
Borrowed from Italian pedale, from Latin pedālis, with a reinterpretation of the Italian ending -ale as the French feminine form of -al. Doublet of pédal.
Borrowed from Italian radice, from Latin rādīx (“root”).
Borrowed from Italian ricotta (literally “cooked again”), from Latin recocta.
Borrowed from Italian ruchetta, diminutive of ruca, from Latin erūca.
Borrowed from Italian rotonda, from Latin rotunda, feminine of rotundus. Doublet of rond.
From Italian saccheggiare, from sacco, from Latin saccus.
From Northern Italian salada, salata (compare insalata), from Vulgar Latin *salāta, from *salō, from Latin saliō, from sal (“salt”).
Borrowed from Italian celata, from Latin caelata.
Borrowed from Italian salto. Doublet of saut.

parole.significato: an Italian police officer of the Middle Ages
parole.testo: Borrowed into Middle French from Italian sbirro, from birro, from Latin birrus (“hooded coat”), related to burrus (“reddish; red-headed”).
Borrowed from Italian scarola, from Latin escāriola.
Borrowed from Italian semola, from Latin simila.
Borrowed from Italian zoccolo (“wooden shoe”), from Latin socculus, diminutive of soccus (“sock”).

parole.significato: pay of a soldier or other military person
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French solde, soulde, borrowed from Italian soldo (“money, pay or salary for a soldier”), from Latin soldus (“solid”), an optional syncope from solidus. Doublet of sou and solide.
Borrowed from Italian soprano, from Vulgar Latin *superanus, from Latin super. Doublet of the inherited souverain.
Borrowed from Italian sottana.

parole.significato: a linen cloth, sometimes entirely of lace or trimmed with lace, used in church sacraments
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French tavaiolle, from Italian tovagliola (“napkin”), diminutive of tovaglia (“tablecloth”), from Medieval Latin toallia, toacula, duvahila, toacla (“towel”), from Frankish *þwahilu (“cloth”). Doublet of touaille.
Borrowed from Italian torrente, from Latin torrentem.
Borrowed from Italian torso, from Latin thyrsus. Doublet of thyrse.
Borrowed from Italian tragetto, from Latin trāiectus, past participle from trāiciō (“transfer, pass through; transfix”).
Borrowed from archaic Italian todesco, from Medieval Latin or Late Latin theodiscus. Doublet of thiois.
Borrowed from Italian tufo.
Borrowed from Italian tenore, from Latin tenorem. Doublet of teneur.
Borrowed from Italian vasca, from Vulgar Latin vāscula, from Latin vāsculum. Compare vaisseau.
Borrowed from Italian vendetta, from Latin vindicta. Doublet of vindicte, borrowed from Latin.
Borrowed from Italian veste.
Borrowed from Italian virtuoso. Doublet of vertueux.

From Old French viste, of disputed origin:. * According to Littré, from Italian visto (“seen”), from Vulgar Latin *visitus, from Latin vidēre. The adverb corresponds with à vue (“rapidly, without notice”); compare Italian avvisto (“noticed, adroit”). * Derived from an onomatopoeia expressing rapid m
Borrowed from Italian veneto, Latin venetus.
Borrowed from Italian zero, alteration of zefiro, from Medieval Latin zephirum, from Arabic صفر. Doublet of chiffre.
Borrowed from Italian manco, from Latin mancus.
From œil + -ade, perhaps an adaptation of Italian occhiata or some other descendant of Vulgar Latin *oculāta. First attested ca. 1480.
